Being alone with women is not a plausible primary trigger for partner violence in a female patient unless there is additional trauma history not represented elsewhere, and military/police uniforms also suggest a different threat context that is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: The memory/appraisal pattern centers on guilt and global identity damage, but the selected triggers point toward external threat cues unrelated to intimate-partner violence. This creates a cross-node mismatch: the triggers imply one trauma context, while memory and appraisals imply another.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is not impossible, but in this profile it intensifies the mismatch because the appraisals are extremely global and identity-based while the trigger content is narrow and externally themed in ways not linked to the romantic-partner abuse formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: Military or police uniforms are not impossible as triggers after intimate partner physical abuse, but in this profile they are hard to justify because no other trigger, memory, threat, appraisal, or strategy item links the trauma to police/military involvement, authority figures, or uniformed responders. issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
issues.explanation: This item is not impossible, but alongside the more specific interpersonal/self-related profile (self-blame, guilt on recall, being alone with men, body-focused avoidance, belonging nowhere), a global 'completely destroyed' worldview reads broader than the rest of the node and may overstate the appraisal pattern relative to the otherwise relationship- and self-focused presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise reflects fear, hypervigilance, avoidance, mistrust, and tension after intimate partner physical abuse. It pulls toward a more disinhibited presentation that is not supported by the trigger, memory, appraisal, or other strategy items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Own Body' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The selected triggers, memories, threats, and appraisals center on interpersonal danger, guilt, and mistrust rather than body-focused trauma responses. This item is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the main formulation compared with the other avoidance item.

vignette:
Leilani was twenty years old, a recent bride and an interior designer just starting to build her client list, when the man she had married began to hurt her. It started with a shove in the kitchen, then a slap that sent her into the wall, then a night when he pinned her down in their dark bedroom and told her she was nothing without him. She left after that night, but the leaving did not end anything. The memory of his hands, his voice in the dark, the way she had frozen—these things stayed. And when she tried to tell her mother what happened, the words fell apart. She would start a sentence and then lose the thread, the room going blurry, and she would stop talking altogether. She felt the guilt like a stone in her chest—she had chosen him, she had stayed too long, she had let it happen. Sometimes, without warning, the full wave of terror would wash over her while she was driving or folding laundry, and there was no image attached, just the body feeling everything again.

She had come to believe that her life was destroyed. She told herself she no longer belonged anywhere—not with her family, who looked at her with pity, and not in the world of other couples, who seemed untouched. People could not be trusted. This belief sat beneath everything. It made her watchful. She walked into a room and scanned every face, every exit, her body constantly tense and ready. She checked behind her when she walked to her car, certain someone was following. When she saw a man who resembled her ex-husband—same build, same jaw—her heart slammed and her throat closed. She had to get out of the store, out of the street, anywhere away.

Being alone with any man now felt impossible. She had stopped meeting new clients in their homes unless another woman was present, and even then she kept the door open. Loud noises made her flinch so hard she dropped things. She avoided the dark altogether—she slept with every light on, and if a bulb burned out she would stay in the living room until morning. She had come to believe that the world was full of threat, and that she had to be ready. This vigilance exhausted her, but it also felt necessary. She was certain that if she let her guard down, something terrible would happen again.

The rumination was constant. She blamed herself for what happened, replaying the moments she could have left, the signs she should have seen. This self-blame fed the guilt that rose when she remembered the event, and the guilt in turn made her want to avoid her own mind. She could not be alone in a room for very long—her thoughts would circle, and the emotion would spike without warning, and she would call her sister or just walk outside. But being alone in the dark was worse, because the memory of that night would surface without an image, just the pressure of his weight and the smell of his breath, and then the guilt would hit again.

The avoidance shaped her life. She turned down a project that required evening site visits. She stopped going to a coffee shop she had loved because a man there had a voice like her ex-husband's. Each time she avoided, she confirmed to herself that she could not handle the world, that her life was narrowed and ruined. The mistrust deepened. She began to believe that her husband had shown her who people really were, and that she had been a fool to think otherwise.

What brought her to therapy was a moment at work. A contractor dropped a metal ladder in the hallway, and the sound sent her into a panic so severe she hid in a supply closet for twenty minutes, shaking. Her boss found her and asked if she was safe. She said yes, but she was not sure she believed it. She was most afraid that she would never feel safe again, that the guilt and the hypervigilance would never stop, that the man who hurt her had taken more than she had realized. But she was also, quietly, hoping that someone could help her find a way back to herself—to the person who had not yet learned to be afraid.
